title: Nov 2024 (Egypt centre)
des: Oman Pearson VUE paediatrics recall, November 2024 (Egypt test centre). Answers checked and explained.

questions.question: A child has fever and signs of meningeal irritation from Haemophilus influenzae type b. Which statement is true?
questions.a: Dexamethasone is harmful in Hib meningitis
questions.d: It does not cause hearing loss
questions.e: The number of cases has fallen sharply since the vaccination programme
questions.exp: Hib conjugate vaccine has almost eliminated invasive Hib disease. Dexamethasone given with the first antibiotic dose reduces hearing loss in Hib meningitis. Test hearing after any bacterial meningitis.

questions.question: Which statement about retinopathy of prematurity is true?
questions.a: ROP is one of the leading causes of preventable childhood blindness
questions.b: Screening is not needed if the baby is well
questions.e: Stage 4 can always be fully treated by laser
questions.exp: ROP remains a leading cause of childhood blindness, especially where preterm survival is rising. Timely screening of babies under 32 weeks or under 1501 g and treatment of type 1 ROP (laser or anti-VEGF) prevent most blindness.

questions.question: What is the most common congenital heart disease?
questions.exp: VSD is the commonest congenital heart lesion (about 30%), most often muscular or perimembranous; many small muscular VSDs close spontaneously.

questions.question: A child has prolonged QT syndrome. Which statement is true?
questions.a: Propranolol (a beta-blocker) is the main treatment
questions.c: It only causes symptoms in adults
questions.e: Digoxin is the drug of choice
questions.exp: Beta-blockers reduce syncope and sudden death in congenital long QT. Avoid QT-prolonging drugs, and correct HYPOkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypocalcaemia. An ICD is used for high-risk patients.

questions.question: Which of these most strongly suggests non-accidental injury?
questions.a: A distal radius buckle fracture in a 7-year-old after a fall
questions.c: A supracondylar fracture after a fall from a climbing frame
questions.d: A toddler's fracture of the tibia in a 2-year-old who walks
questions.e: A clavicle fracture after a difficult delivery
questions.exp: Long bone fractures in non-mobile infants are highly suspicious of abuse unless there is a clear, consistent explanation (such as birth injury or bone disease). Do a skeletal survey and safeguarding assessment.

questions.question: Which complication can follow surfactant administration?
questions.exp: After surfactant, falling pulmonary vascular resistance can increase left-to-right ductal flow and cause pulmonary haemorrhage. Wean ventilation quickly as compliance improves to avoid air leak.

questions.question: An antenatal scan showed unilateral hydronephrosis (pelvis over 10 mm) with a normal opposite kidney. After birth the baby passes urine well and feeds well. What should be done?
questions.d: Renal ultrasound after 72 hours of life (day 3–7)
questions.exp: Unilateral antenatal hydronephrosis with a normal other kidney: scan after 48–72 hours (earlier scans underestimate dilatation because newborns are relatively dehydrated). Urgent day-1 scans are for bilateral hydronephrosis, a solitary kidney or suspected posterior urethral valves in boys. Antibiotic prophylaxis depends on the degree.

questions.question: A growth chart shows height falling across centiles while weight is maintained. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Endocrine causes (hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, Cushing) slow height more than weight. Malnutrition and gut disease (coeliac, Crohn's) reduce weight first.

questions.question: When does a healthy baby usually double his birth weight?
questions.exp: Birth weight doubles at about 4–5 months and triples at 1 year.

questions.question: A child has recurrent skin abscesses, liver abscesses and suppurative lymphadenitis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: CGD: deep abscesses (liver, lung, lymph nodes, skin, bone) with catalase-positive organisms (Staph aureus, Serratia, Aspergillus). Test with DHR flow cytometry.

questions.question: A child with congenital adrenal hyperplasia is on hydrocortisone. What is the effect of too LITTLE treatment?
questions.a: Weight gain with short stature from excess cortisol
questions.c: Faster growth with accelerated bone maturation (from excess androgens)
questions.exp: Under-treatment lets ACTH drive adrenal androgens: tall for age early, advanced bone age, early fusion and short adult height, with virilisation. Over-treatment slows growth and causes cushingoid features.

questions.question: An athlete has hyperkalaemia (K 9 mmol/L) after vigorous exercise. Which treatment lowers the potassium most effectively and quickly?
questions.exp: Insulin with glucose and nebulised salbutamol shift potassium into cells within 15–30 minutes (insulin is the most reliable). Calcium gluconate protects the heart but does not lower potassium. Resins and diuretics remove potassium slowly; dialysis for refractory cases. Exercise-induced rhabdomyolysis can cause this.

questions.question: Which hormone drives the complications of refeeding syndrome?
questions.exp: Carbohydrate refeeding releases insulin, driving phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells and retaining sodium and water.

questions.question: A 3-day-old has purulent conjunctivitis. What is the most important treatment?
questions.exp: Purulent conjunctivitis at 2–5 days is presumed gonococcal: systemic ceftriaxone plus saline irrigation, test for chlamydia, and treat the parents.

questions.question: A child was briefly submerged and now has a cough and has vomited. He is alert with normal vital signs (BP 110/80). What should be done?
questions.exp: Lung injury after drowning can appear hours later. Observe at least 6–8 hours with saturations; discharge if normal.

questions.question: A boy bleeds after circumcision. The APTT is markedly prolonged while PT and thrombin time are normal. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: An isolated long APTT with bleeding in a boy suggests haemophilia A (factor VIII, most common) or B (factor IX). Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the PT first; factor VII deficiency prolongs only the PT; factor XIII deficiency gives normal tests.

questions.question: An adolescent boy has died in the emergency department, and the family were not present. How should they be told?
questions.a: Let the nurse tell them in the corridor
questions.d: In a private room, sitting down, after calmly explaining that there is bad news
questions.e: Over the phone as soon as possible
questions.exp: Break bad news face to face in a private, quiet room, sitting down, with a warning shot and clear words ("he has died"), allowing time for questions and offering support.

questions.question: A boy on imipramine has a QRS over 140 ms with a prolonged PR and tachycardia. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Tricyclic toxicity with a wide QRS needs IV sodium bicarbonate (1–2 mmol/kg), aiming for a pH of 7.45–7.55.

questions.question: A child has chest pain and fever, and the ECG shows widespread ST elevation with PR depression. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Acute pericarditis: diffuse concave ST elevation and PR depression, pleuritic pain relieved by sitting forward, a pericardial rub. Echo for effusion and tamponade.

questions.question: A cyanosed infant's chest X-ray shows a "figure of 8" or "snowman" heart. What is the diagnosis?
questions.b: Supracardiac total anomalous pulmonary venous return
questions.exp: In supracardiac TAPVR, the pulmonary veins drain via a vertical vein to the innominate vein and SVC, which form the upper part of the snowman. ToF is boot-shaped, TGA is "egg on a string", Ebstein is a huge box-shaped heart.

questions.question: A 2-year-old girl has had delayed motor milestones since 6 months and delayed speech. What is the initial assessment?
questions.c: Vision and hearing assessment (with a full developmental and physical examination)
questions.exp: Global developmental delay needs hearing and vision checks first, a full history and examination (head circumference, dysmorphism, neurocutaneous signs), then first-line tests such as chromosomal microarray, fragile X, thyroid function and CK in boys with motor delay; MRI and metabolic tests are guided by findings.

questions.question: A teenager took aspirin in a suicide attempt 45 minutes ago. What is the management?
questions.e: A single dose of activated charcoal, with salicylate levels
questions.exp: Activated charcoal within 1 hour, serial salicylate levels and blood gases, IV bicarbonate for urinary alkalinisation in moderate poisoning, and haemodialysis for severe poisoning. All self-poisonings need a psychosocial assessment.

questions.question: A toddler with cyanotic breath-holding spells has jerking movements during the attacks. Which test is useful?
questions.exp: Brief anoxic jerks in breath-holding spells are not epilepsy. Iron deficiency is common and iron reduces attacks. An ECG is advised if attacks are atypical.

questions.question: A newborn has SpO2 95% and a heart rate of 90/min but is breathing only 4 times a minute. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Apnoea with a heart rate under 100 needs ventilation, starting in air for term babies.

questions.question: A child has abnormal liver tests, and the mother says privately that her child swallowed a drug. Which drug is the most likely cause and what is the treatment?
questions.a: Paracetamol; give N-acetylcysteine guided by the level and timing
questions.exp: Paracetamol overdose causes hepatotoxicity 24–72 hours after ingestion. Measure the level at 4 hours (or at presentation if later) and give NAC if above the treatment line, if the timing is unknown, or if liver tests are abnormal.

questions.question: A paediatric resident with many duty hours develops burnout. What is a likely consequence?
questions.a: Unprofessional behaviour and more medical errors
questions.exp: Burnout (emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation, low sense of achievement) is linked to medical errors, poorer professionalism and communication, and leaving medicine. Systems should limit hours, provide support and supervision, and promote wellbeing.

questions.question: Which electrolyte findings are typical of pyloric stenosis?
questions.a: Low chloride, low potassium and metabolic alkalosis
questions.exp: Vomiting stomach acid causes hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria. Correct fluids and electrolytes (chloride over 100, bicarbonate under 26) before pyloromyotomy.

questions.question: A well-hydrated, well neonate with Down syndrome has a total bilirubin of 20 mg/dL (340 micromol/L). What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Treat according to gestation- and age-specific thresholds (NICE or AAP charts). At this level in a well term baby beyond 48 hours, phototherapy is indicated; exchange is for levels above the exchange line or signs of encephalopathy. Check thyroid function in babies with Down syndrome and prolonged jaundice.

questions.question: A macrosomic 4.2 kg infant of a diabetic mother was admitted with respiratory distress. Three weeks later he has a systolic murmur at the left sternal border. What is the most likely cause?
questions.a: Septal hypertrophy (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy of the IDM)
questions.exp: Septal hypertrophy is common in IDMs and may cause left ventricular outflow obstruction; it regresses over months. Avoid inotropes; propranolol if obstructive.

questions.question: A 14-year-old boy is depressed after his parents' divorce and has lost interest in his hobbies. What is the most important thing to ask him?
questions.b: His relationship with his parents only
questions.c: Whether he wants a new phone
questions.e: Whether he has thoughts that life is not worth living or of harming himself
questions.exp: Every young person with low mood should be asked directly about suicidal thoughts, plans and self-harm; asking does not increase risk. Also assess safety, support, substance use and school, using a HEADSSS approach.

questions.question: A neonate has acidosis, a very high ammonia and a high anion gap. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Organic acidaemias (methylmalonic, propionic) cause high anion gap acidosis with ketosis and hyperammonaemia. Urea cycle defects cause hyperammonaemia without acidosis. PKU does not cause acute neonatal illness.

questions.question: A child with recurrent otitis media has a chronic ear discharge through a perforated drum. What is the treatment?
questions.b: Topical ciprofloxacin drops with aural cleaning
questions.exp: Chronic suppurative otitis media is treated with aural toilet and topical quinolone drops (not ototoxic). Persistent cases need ENT review (cholesteatoma, tympanoplasty).

questions.question: A mother had Graves disease treated by thyroidectomy and now takes thyroxine. Her TSH-receptor antibodies are still high. How should her baby be screened?
questions.b: Serial thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4) in the first weeks
questions.e: No screening is needed because she had surgery
questions.exp: After thyroidectomy or radioiodine, TRAb can persist and cross the placenta, causing fetal and neonatal thyrotoxicosis even though the mother is euthyroid on thyroxine. Check the baby's TFTs (and TRAb) at day 3–5 and 10–14, and watch for tachycardia, poor weight gain and irritability.

questions.question: A baby is in shock and no IV line can be inserted. What should be done?
questions.c: Insert a central line under ultrasound first
questions.e: Keep trying peripheral lines for 30 minutes
questions.exp: If IV access fails within about 1–2 attempts or 90 seconds in a critically ill child, insert an IO needle (proximal tibia); all fluids and drugs can be given.

questions.question: A 14-year-old has frequent blinking and repeated throat-clearing noises for more than a year. They come and go and increase with stress. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Tourette syndrome: multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic for over a year, starting before 18. Tics wax and wane and can be briefly suppressed. Common comorbidities are ADHD and OCD. Treat with education and habit-reversal therapy; clonidine or aripiprazole if severe.

questions.question: A child has vomiting, nausea and abdominal pain. The abdominal X-ray shows radio-opaque tablets in the stomach (left hypochondrium). Iron poisoning is suspected. What is the specific treatment?
questions.exp: Iron tablets are radio-opaque. Iron poisoning causes vomiting, GI bleeding, then a latent phase, then shock, acidosis and liver failure. Measure serum iron at 4 hours; give IV desferrioxamine for systemic toxicity or high levels; whole bowel irrigation if many tablets are seen. Charcoal does not bind iron.

questions.question: After tonsillectomy, a child with untreated hyperthyroidism develops a thyroid storm with fever of 39°C and a heart rate of 170/min. What should be given?
questions.exp: Thyroid storm: give a beta-blocker (propranolol) for adrenergic symptoms, a thionamide (PTU blocks T4 to T3 conversion as well), then iodide an hour later, steroids, and cooling with paracetamol. Avoid aspirin, which displaces thyroid hormone from its binding protein.
